A waistcoat is a sleeveless, button-up garment that covers only your torso — from your shoulders down to roughly your waist or hips. It has no sleeves at all, and it typically has a V-shaped opening at the top (the neckline). It is designed to be worn over a shirt but under a jacket.

Picture a regular shirt. Now mentally remove both sleeves entirely, shorten it so it ends around your waist, add a row of buttons running down the center of the front, and make it fit quite snugly against the body. That's a waistcoat.

A few more physical details:

  • The front is usually made of a smart, often patterned or solid-colored fabric.
  • The back is typically made of a simpler, thinner material (often a satin-like lining), since it's hidden by the jacket anyway.
  • It almost always has small pockets on the front, sometimes including a tiny pocket specifically for a pocket watch.
  • It buttons all the way from the collar down to the hem.

The classic way to wear a waistcoat is as part of what is called a three-piece suit: trousers + waistcoat + jacket, all made from the same fabric. When you wear all three together, the waistcoat fills the gap between your shirt and jacket, giving the outfit a layered, polished, formal appearance. It also keeps the shirt tucked in neatly and adds warmth.

However, waistcoats are also worn without a jacket — just over a shirt — especially in business settings or as a fashion choice.

Waistcoats are associated with formal and smart occasions: weddings, job interviews, business meetings, dinners, or any event where dressing up is expected. That said, waistcoats have also become a popular everyday fashion item in recent decades, worn more casually with jeans or trousers.

Traditionally, waistcoats were a staple of men's formal fashion, and they remain so. But women wear them too — both as part of tailored suits and as standalone fashion pieces. There is no strict rule about gender here in modern usage.
A very important note: British vs. American English

This is crucial to know:

  • In British English, the garment is called a waistcoat.
  • In American English, the exact same garment is called a vest.

So if you read an American novel and it says a character is wearing a "vest" over their shirt and under their jacket, it's describing a waistcoat. The word "vest" in British English, on the other hand, refers to an undershirt (a plain garment worn under a shirt, closest to the skin) — which is completely different. This difference trips up many learners and even native speakers crossing between the two dialects.

• He arrived at the wedding in a charcoal grey three-piece suit, his waistcoat perfectly buttoned.
  • She wore a floral waistcoat over a white blouse, without a jacket.
  • The tailor adjusted the waistcoat so it sat flat against his chest.
  • He pulled out his pocket watch from the small waistcoat pocket.

A waistcoat is a sleeveless, button-front garment worn over a shirt, covering the torso. It is a formal or smart piece of clothing, most famously worn as the middle layer of a three-piece suit. In American English, the same thing is called a vest.
